article.title: Serious Car Accident
article.author: Sejal Desai
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The first 24 hours after a serious accident in Houston can be the difference between injuries being properly treated and critical evidence surviving. Traffic might be moving around the wrecked cars. Emergency personnel might be separating the drivers. Pain might make it hard to think clearly. Safety, then medical care, then meticulous documentation. Once urgent needs are addressed, a Houston car accident lawyer can examine the crash record, insurance issues, and losses that begin accumulating immediately. The injured person still has useful steps to take before memories fade or vehicles are repaired. Move to Safety and Report the Crash Call 911 when anyone may be injured, or the collision blocks traffic. If the vehicles can be moved safely, Texas law generally requires drivers to clear certain crashes from the main roadway. Hazard lights, a safe shoulder, or a nearby parking area can reduce the chance of a second impact. Give the responding officer accurate facts without guessing about speed, distance, or fault. The Texas Department of Transportation maintains the state crash-record system and explains how people can obtain reports. Record the agency name, incident number, and officer’s information so the report can be requested later. If police cannot respond, exchange the required information and ask how to make an official report. Write down the exact location and time. A screenshot of the map position can help when frontage roads, ramps, or large intersections make the location difficult to describe later. Accept Medical Assessment Adrenaline can hide pain after a violent impact. Head injuries, internal bleeding, and spinal trauma may not produce obvious symptoms at the scene. Tell paramedics about dizziness, confusion, numbness, breathing problems, or pain anywhere in the body. Follow their recommendation about transport. If an ambulance is unnecessary, seek medical evaluation as soon as practical. Describe how the crash occurred and every symptom, even one that seems minor. Early records help clinicians assess changes and connect later findings to the collision. Keep discharge instructions, prescriptions, work restrictions, and referral information together. Preserve the Scene You Can See Take photographs or video only when it is safe. Capture vehicle positions, damage, debris, skid marks, traffic controls, road conditions, and nearby businesses that may have cameras. Wide views show the setting, while closer images preserve details such as broken lights or tire marks. Exchange names, contact details, driver’s license information, license plates, and insurance information. Ask witnesses for their contact details rather than relying on the police report to identify everyone. Do not argue with the other driver or post conclusions about fault online. Protect Time-Sensitive Evidence Some evidence disappears quickly. Store cameras may overwrite footage within days. Damaged vehicles may be repaired, sold, or salvaged. Electronic information from a vehicle can also be lost if no one sends a preservation request. Write down the route, direction of travel, traffic signal, weather, and what happened before impact. Save dashcam files in more than one place. Photograph visible injuries over the following days, since bruising and swelling can change. Keep damaged personal property if it may help explain the force of the collision. Notify Insurers With Care Make sure to notify your insurer of the collision within the time limit stipulated by your policy. Give the basic facts needed to open the claim. Do not estimate the severity of an injury or agree to a recorded statement until you understand the request. A statement made under medication, fatigue, or uncertainty can result in unnecessary arguments. Don't sign a blanket medical authorization or take a quick settlement without seeing what it covers. An initial offer might take care of the car damage, but not the medical bills. Ask the adjuster to put the requests and decisions in writing. Keep the damaged vehicle available until necessary photographs and inspections are complete. If storage fees are growing, document the vehicle thoroughly and ask what preservation steps are needed before authorizing repairs or disposal. Begin a Simple Loss File Create one place for medical records, photographs, receipts, correspondence, and claim numbers. Note missed work, canceled jobs, transportation expenses, and help needed at home. A short daily account of pain, sleep, mobility, and treatment can preserve details that are hard to recall months later. The first 24 hours do not decide every legal issue, yet they often supply the earliest reliable evidence. Prompt care and orderly records give medical providers, insurers, and later reviewers a clearer account of the crash and its effects.
